title: Microbatch economics playlet — seller notes (draft)
content:
Purpose:
Quick, seller-facing playlet that explains the value and tradeoffs of enabling microbatching for customer pilots. Target audience: SEs and sellers running 1:1 pilot and early pilot-to-production conversations with platform and product engineering teams.

TL;DR (elevator lines for sellers) — use one of these depending on persona:
- For Integration Leads (latency-focused): "Microbatching gives you up to 35% token-cost savings while keeping median tail latency within your 99th percentile SLA by batching opportunistically behind an adaptive latency budget."
- For Platform / Infra (cost-focused): "Microbatching is an operational lever to reduce per-request token spend and GPU utilization without changing model family — we’ll show an A/B pilot with real traffic to quantify dollars saved."
- For Product PMs (accuracy-sensitive): "Microbatching is a throughput optimization; we preserve deterministic ordering and KV cache integrity so accuracy is unchanged if latency bounds are respected. We’ll validate with your prompt set."

What this playlet contains (quick index):
1) Short script + one-pager seller pitch (this doc)
2) SE integration checklist (small checklist to run pilot)
3) Pilot metrics to collect (baseline vs microbatch)
4) Demo scripts and failover cases
5) Objection responses + battlecard bullets
6) Quick economics examples (ballpark numbers)
7) Open questions and next steps / handoff notes

SE integration checklist (minimal, consult infra for dedicated customers):
- Confirm model family and expected sequence lengths (p95 tokens). If > 512 p95, call out memory plan.
- Confirm route(s) for pilot traffic and whether routing policy allows temporary 30–200ms queuing.
- Set microbatch policy: target batch max latency = desired SLO headroom (e.g., if 99p SLO = 450ms, set microbatch headroom = 80–120ms).
- Enable KV/prefix caching on the model route and pin same model version for test.
- Instrument per-request latency histogram (p50/p90/p95/p99), token counts, GPU utilization, and per-request cost estimate.
- Add a simple fallback route that disables batching (route B) and a canary traffic rule (5–10% to route B for first 24h).
- Prepare prompt set (30–200 representative prompts) for QA to check content parity.

Pilot metrics (collect these for 72 hours at both baseline and microbatch config):
- Effective tokens per second (tokens/s) and tokens per GPU second
- Mean and tail latencies (p50/p90/p95/p99) end-to-end
- 95th latency delta after batching enabled
- Cost per 1k tokens (or per request) as shown in console
- Model output regression checks (BLEU/ROUGE-ish or simple pass/fail on assert prompts)
- Failure modes: queued request throttles, early cancellations, KV mismatches

Quick economics examples (ballpark — use real telemetry for final numbers):
- Example A (low-latency chat agent): baseline avg tokens/request = 120 tokens; model throughput without batching = 15 req/s; cost = $0.020 per 1k tokens. With microbatching we increase token efficiency by 28% (shared decode work + continuous batching), so effective cost drop ~22% and GPU utilization down by 25%. If customer is running 1M requests/mo, this is ~ $440/mo savings at baseline assumptions.
- Example B (high-throughput summarization): baseline avg tokens/request = 600; batching is more effective (40–55% savings), so if baseline $2,400/mo for model usage, microbatching can save ~ $1k/mo.
- Note: these are conservative estimates; dedicated customers with longer sequences see bigger wins. Always run pilot.

Demo script (SE-friendly, ~6–8 mins):
1) Show baseline run: route = model:prod-no-batch, record p95 and token cost.
2) Flip config to microbatch policy (route = model:microbatch-1), show live dashboard: batching percentage, mean batch size, queue latency percentiles.
3) Run sample prompt set and show content parity (side-by-side).
4) Trigger a controlled load spike (locally or via jmeter) and show fallback to non-batched route (route B) or quick throttle threshold.
5) Summarize savings using console econ chart.

Quick fallback / canary play (step-by-step):
- Day 0: Config live in dev and SE demo only.
- Day 1 (pilot start): 10% traffic to batch route, 90% baseline. Monitor errors and p99 drift closely for first 2 hours.
- If p99 latency increases >20% or error rate > baseline + 0.5% absolute, roll back to baseline (manual) and capture logs (trace ids).
- After 24h stable, increase to 50% / 50% and run full prompt regression.
- After 72h stable and validated content parity + econ win, propose production rollout with 3-tier ramp and persistent fallback route.

Seller objection responses (rapid bullets):
- "Batching will change results" — We only batch at the decode stage and respect request order and KV cache semantics; we validate against your prompts in the pilot and provide a canary route that has batching disabled.
- "Latency spikes are unacceptable" — We honor a per-request latency budget and will configure microbatch headroom; you can always opt for fallback route that disables microbatching.
- "We can build this ourselves" — You could, but our runtime bundles batching, KV cache safety, and cost accounting with rollout policies and perf dashboards. That saves months and reduces ops risk.
- "How does this affect token accounting/pricing?" — Token accounting is unchanged; you’ll see reduced spend because fewer decode cycles and improved GPU utilization. We'll show concrete per-1k token numbers in the pilot.

Rapid playbook for contract conversations (seller cheats):
- Offer a 6-week microbatch pilot with three checkpoints (week 1 baseline instrumentation, week 3 mid-rollout, week 6 handoff + economic report).
- Include an explicit rollback SLA in the pilot statement of work: customer can ask to disable batching within 2 hours of request.
- Suggest a small Dedicated burst credit if they need higher concurrency during pilot (cost mitigation).

Ops/engineering guardrails (notes to SEs):
- Watch memory pressure on GPUs — batching increases peak memory use if multiple large sequences are collocated. Tune max batch size and sequence padding heuristics.
- Ensure quantization or kernel changes are identical between routes. Differences confound regressions.
- Prefer token-length bucketing when possible to keep batch variance low.

Open questions / risks to document before next review:
- How often will we surface per-request batch attribution in console (need trace-level linking)? Related CONFLUENCE-5642.
- Should we enable automatic batch-size auto-tuning in Dedicated pilots, or keep manual knob for first 90 days?
- Data residency note for Private deployments: microbatching implies request coalescing — confirm inter-region routing constraints for regulated customers.

Next steps (owner: Maya Chen) — sprint actions:
- [ ] Finalize SE checklist and convert to a short Playbook PDF (deadline 2025-09-08).
- [ ] Run two internal microbatch A/Bs with sample app (Jordan) and capture econ deltas (due 2025-09-05).
- [ ] Create a short one-slide flow diagram for seller deck (Priya).
- [ ] Add a stubbed canary run script to github repo (Carlos) and link PR (JIRA-GTM-1123).

Notes to self (informal):
- Keep language light and focused on dollars + risk mitigation — sellers want quick win narratives.
- Avoid heavy infra jargon in external-facing slide; move that to SE appendix.

End of draft — comments welcome.
